other_side: Zitron attacks the same OpenAI research this edition is built on, and goes after its central instrument: the token. He argues token counts measure subsidy rather than work, since customers still "burn anywhere from $20 to $40 in tokens for every dollar of software spend", and he notes that when OpenAI and Anthropic moved larger companies onto token-based billing this year, "enterprises almost immediately started cutting token budgets" because "nobody could actually point to anything improving". He then turns OpenAI's own economists against the headline: buried on page 35 of their 69-page report is the finding that "revenue per employee is not meaningfully associated with output tokens per employee" — so a firm burning eight times the tokens is not demonstrably eight times more productive. On agents he doubts the delegation story itself, describing the typical rig as "a contrived series of harnesses, prompts, API calls and burned tokens" that "requires constant maintenance to do some stuff sometimes".
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether output tokens are a valid proxy for work done. Both accept the same facts: frontier-firm token use really has grown roughly seventeen-fold, agentic traffic really is most of enterprise output, and adoption really is lopsided between firms. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the token gap ever shows up in outputs — the specific observable is revenue, margin or headcount per employee for the heavy-agentic cohort against their sector peers over the next few years, which is precisely the correlation OpenAI's own economists could not find. The residue is pure worldview: Whittemore reads high token burn as capability being exercised, Zitron reads it as an inefficient product being subsidised. Whittemore is vindicated if the 8.3X cohort visibly outperforms on ordinary business measures once inference is no longer sold below cost; Zitron if usage stays high while performance stays flat and budgets are cut at renewal. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: neither disputes that adoption is now real, broad and very unevenly distributed. Watch for anyone publishing an outcome measure, rather than a usage measure, for the frontier cohort.
